source_text: Et ubi est crimen tuum diabolicum, quod illi argumento pudoris nitebaris affigere? Non enim iam libido reprehenditur, quae et in prohibito et in concesso usu, naturae ipsius conditione sentitur, si depravatio eius, ad id quod non licebat excurrens, sola culpatur.
pass_a_gloss: And where is your diabolical charge, which you were striving to fasten on that argument of modesty? For lust is not now blamed, which is felt both in a forbidden and in a granted use by the condition of nature itself, if its depravation, running out to that which was not allowed, alone is faulted.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Where, then, is your diabolical crime, which you tried to attach to it through the argument from shame? Sexual desire itself is no longer being condemned—the desire felt by nature’s own constitution in both forbidden and permitted intercourse—if only its distortion, straying toward what is unlawful, is blamed.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Augustine's quoted claim that the unbaptized remain under the devil; keep the personal devil, not 'evil'.
rejected: under Satan (name not in the Latin here)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
